source: Solving Elastic Collisions
Combine conservation of momentum and of kinetic energy: the relative speed reverses in a one-dimensional elastic collision.
Students write only the momentum equation and are left with one equation for two unknowns.

Elastic and Inelastic Collisions defined an elastic collision as one that keeps the total kinetic energy. Solving one means handling two equations at once, one of them quadratic, which is a job for Nonlinear Systems. A clever division turns it into two linear equations.

For masses $m_1, m_2$ with velocities $v_1, v_2$ before and $v_1', v_2'$ after, move each object's terms to its own side: $$m_1(v_1 - v_1') = m_2(v_2' - v_2) \quad\text{(momentum)},$$ $$m_1(v_1^2 - v_1'^2) = m_2(v_2'^2 - v_2^2) \quad\text{(kinetic energy, times 2)}.$$ Factor the squares, $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, and divide the second equation by the first (the collision happened, so $v_1 \ne v_1'$): $$v_1 + v_1' = v_2 + v_2' \;\Rightarrow\; v_2' - v_1' = -(v_2 - v_1).$$

In a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative velocity reverses: the objects separate as fast as they approached. Together with momentum conservation, that gives $$v_1' = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1 + \dfrac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_2, \qquad v_2' = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_1 + \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_2.$$
A $2\ \text{kg}$ glider at $6\ \text{m/s}$ hits a $4\ \text{kg}$ glider at rest: it bounces back at $2\ \text{m/s}$ while the other moves off at $4\ \text{m/s}$.
A $2\ \text{kg}$ glider at $6\ \text{m/s}$ collides elastically with a $4\ \text{kg}$ glider at rest. Find both velocities afterward.
A light glider hits a heavy one
$v_1' = -2\ \text{m/s}$ (it bounces back), $v_2' = 4\ \text{m/s}$.
Relative velocity reverses: $v_2' - v_1' = 6$.
Check the energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(36) = 36\ \text{J}$ before; $\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(4) + \tfrac{1}{2}(4)(16) = 4 + 32 = 36\ \text{J}$ after.
A $3\ \text{kg}$ cart at $4\ \text{m/s}$ meets a $1\ \text{kg}$ cart moving toward it at $2\ \text{m/s}$. The collision is elastic. Find the velocities afterward.
Head-on, both moving
$v_1' = 1\ \text{m/s}$, $v_2' = 7\ \text{m/s}$, both in the positive direction.
Take the 3 kg cart's direction as positive: $v_1 = 4$, $v_2 = -2$. Momentum: $3v_1' + v_2' = 12 - 2 = 10$.
Relative velocity: $v_2' - v_1' = 4 - (-2) = 6$.

Writing only the momentum equation. With two unknown final velocities, one equation can't decide them; any pair on a line works, including ones that create energy. Check: count unknowns and equations. For an elastic collision use momentum plus the reversal of relative velocity (which is energy conservation in disguise); for a perfectly inelastic one, use momentum plus "same final velocity."
